chunks: Improving buck efficiency at light load. The question: What can you do to increase efficiency at light loads?
At light load the converter delivers very little power, so even small fixed losses become a large share of it.
The energy to flip the switches each cycle (gate drive and switching loss) and the controller's own supply current are paid whether or not the load is big.
To improve efficiency you attack those fixed costs. The main tools are skipping pulses, turning the low-side switch off at zero current, and cutting quiescent current.
Think of a car idling at a red light. The engine burns fuel just to stay on, even though the car goes nowhere. If you only look at distance per liter, idling looks terrible.
The fix is to shut the engine off between uses, which is what a burst mode does. The analogy breaks down in that a buck can wake up in microseconds, while a car engine cannot.
Forced PWM (red) is below 10% at 100 microamps and only reaches 41% at 10 milliamps. PFM (orange) removes most of the loss, plateauing near 91%.
At microamp loads the plateau gives way to the sleep-current term, which is why cutting I q from 20 microamps to 2 microamps (blue vs green) matters below about 1 milliamps.
A larger inductor (green vs orange) lifts the whole plateau because each pulse carries more charge.
Light load: a small output current compared with the converter's rating. Fixed losses: losses that do not shrink with load, such as gate drive and quiescent current.
Quiescent current ( I Q ): the current the controller draws just to stay alive. PFM / burst mode: firing pulses only when needed ("Explain PFM operation in a buck").
Diode emulation: turning the bottom switch off at zero current so no current flows backward ("DCM vs CCM in a buck converter").
A converter outputs 3. 3 volts at 10 milliamps, which is 33 milliwatts. Its fixed losses are 30 milliwatts.
The input power is 63 milliwatts, so efficiency is 33 over 63 about 52 % . Cut the fixed losses to 3 milliwatts with burst mode and low quiescent current.
Now the input is 36 milliwatts and efficiency is 33 over 36 about 92 % . That is the whole idea.
"At light load the losses that don't scale with load, gate drive, switch-node capacitance and quiescent current, dominate the efficiency number.

So you cut them: use PFM or burst mode so pulses and switching losses scale with load, diode emulation so you don't circulate reverse current, a low-quiescent-current controller and a high-value feedback divider, and in multiphase designs shed phases.
At microamp loads an ultra-low- I q LDO can win. The trade-offs are more ripple and slower first response."
